en: Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati; salutations! Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gurus!
Whose form is an unbroken circle, pervading all that is moving and unmoving.
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that state has been revealed.
That reality is inexpressible and unheard, beyond the sphere of speech and mind.
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that very reality has been fully attained.
With the ointment-stick of knowledge for the world blinded by ignorance,
Salutation to that glorious Guru by whom the eye has been opened.
Endowed with the power of knowledge and adorned with a garland of principles (tattvas).
I salute the Guru, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation, who is like Śiva himself.
The guru, the even more venerable one, and those others who are elder brothers.
I also bow to the others who are successively superior, ending with Viśuddhānna.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara.
The Guru is God; to that Śrī Guru, who is the entire universe, salutations.
O Lord, grant me the favor of your command; by your grace, I have attained perfection.
Having performed the recitation of my names, grant me your blessing.
Illuminating the expanse of the sky with its unbroken, circular form.
That is declared to be immovable; this is established in the immovable.
To the sole cause for destroying the terrible disease of beginningless saṃsāra.
Homage to the illustrious Lord Physician, the provider of the medicine of primordial wisdom.
Then, at the time of the rising of the elder brother of Garuḍa, having risen and sat down...
Upon the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of one's own head.
Cool, resembling a white lotus, with a face like the autumn moon.
Adorned with a pair of eyes having the form of full-blown blue lotuses.
With a gentle smile, wearing white garments, and anointed with white perfumes and unguents.
His chest is adorned with a white garland, and he shines with two arms graced by the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
His body is embraced by his own Śakti, who rests upon his left lap and holds a red lotus with her right hand.
His mind was delighted by the nectar of the lotus of wisdom.
Having meditated upon one's own guru: "O Amukānandanātha and Amukaśaktyāmbā, I worship the pair of your venerable sandals."

Having thus worshipped with mental perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and flowers; having prostrated; having offered praise; and having requested permission to perform the daily rites (*nityakarman*), one should bid farewell to the venerable Guru in the place of Viṣṇu and engage in the recitation of mantras for the sake of what is necessary.
[Thus ends the first section: The Manual for the Meditation on the Guru.]

Having gone outside, facing either south or north, and having covered his mouth with his right hand, he should remain silent. After voiding feces and urine, he should rise, take earth from a barren spot of ground, go near water, and perform purification: one application of earth for the penis and one for the anus.

Fifteen [applications of earth] on the left hand, and likewise seven on both hands; this is prescribed as the rule for purification with earth. Having performed purification in this manner, having washed both hands and feet, and having cleansed the mouth with water, one should use a tooth-stick.

Taking branches from the *apāmārga*, *udumbara*, *khadira*, *jambūka*, thorny trees, or those that are bitter, astringent, or pungent, one should prepare a tooth-stick by cutting it to a length of twelve finger-breadths.
[The following] are forbidden: on the new moon day (*āmāvāsyā*), the eighth, the fourteenth, the sixth, the first, and the eleventh days. These [days are forbidden].

On these days, one should not use a tooth-stick. Again, taking water, one should perform seven mouthfuls of rinsing (*gaṇḍūṣa*). Having washed both hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), [one should recite]: *oṃ vaṃ varuṇāya jalādhipataye mama vākkāyakarmapāpāni saṃhara (2) oṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus.
Having recited the mantra seven times, one should perform the bath; then, taking again the clay from the Gaṅgā.
Having recited the mantra.
O Earth, traversed by Viṣṇu, traversed by the chariot, traversed by the horse!
Whatever evil was conceived by my mind, whatever misdeed was committed by me;
Having performed the ritual bath with mantras.

Having put on his garment and performed the remembrance of the Guru with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, and vermilion, he should place them upon his head and apply a tilaka mark on his forehead.
Then, in a pure place— whether by a riverbank, in a temple, or in one's own home—
Having smeared the place chosen for the mind with cow dung, one should prepare a seat— either a black antelope skin, a tiger skin, a red woolen blanket, or a silk cloth— as available.
Facing the east, having sat upon a lotus seat, and having performed the root-lock (mūlabandha).

Gazing at the space between the eyebrows, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*. Having drawn [the air] in through the left nostril sixteen times with the seed-syllable of air, *oṃ yaṃ*, one should dry up the body. Having retained [the breath] through the *suṣumṇā* sixty-four times with the seed-syllable of fire, *oṃ raṃ*, one should burn the body. *Oṃ...*

By raining down with the nectar-seed syllable *vaṃ* located at the forehead, one should exhale through the right nostril thirty-two times. Having solidified the body with the earth-seed syllable *oṃ laṃ*,
and having meditated upon oneself as the form of the deity, this is the accomplishment of the elements (*bhūtasiddhi*).
Brahmā is to be known as the inhaler (pūraka), while Viṣṇu is said to be the retainer (kuṃbhaka).
Recaka is likewise to be known as the supreme Śiva, who is both perishable and imperishable.

Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) in this manner: Oṃ, salutation to the venerable gurus (*śrīgurubhyaḥ*). Oṃ, salutation to the venerable supreme gurus (*śrīparamagurubhyaḥ*). Oṃ, salutation to the venerable preceptor-gurus (*parameṣṭhigurubhyaḥ*). Oṃ, salutation to the venerable higher-lower gurus (*śrīparāparagurubhyaḥ*). Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Tejānandanātha. Oṃ Hrīṃ...

To the thousand-rayed Sūrya, protect my self, svāhā! This is the mantra for self-protection. Oṃ hrāṃ, homage to Sūrya with the two thumbs; oṃ hrīṃ, homage to the Lord of Splendor with the two index fingers; oṃ hrūṃ...

Oṃ *bhāskarāya* madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ. Oṃ *hraim* *dinakarāya* anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ. Oṃ *hrauṃ* *tapanāya* kaniṣṭhikābhyāṃ namaḥ. Oṃ *hraḥ* *tamovairiṇe* karatalakara-pṛṣṭābhyāṃ namaḥ. Oṃ *hrāṃ* *caṇḍaraśmaye* hṛdayāya namaḥ. Oṃ *hrīṃ*.
Svāhā to the most excellent head. Oṃ hrūṃ, vauṣaṭ to the Lord’s crest-lock. Oṃ hraiṃ, hūṃ to the light of the armor. Oṃ hrauṃ, vaṣaṭ to the lotus-handed one and the three eyes.
Oṃ hraḥ, phaṭ to the single-wheeled one and the weapon-mantra. Again, having drawn a square mandala, [place it] in the center.

Having drawn a triangle, a hexagon, and a circle, and provided them with scents, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, [one should recite]: *oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ ādhāraśakti agnimaṇḍalāya daśakalātmane namaḥ*. Thus is the worship of the support (*ādhāra-pūjā*).

Then, taking a copper vessel together with scents, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, [one should recite]: *oṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya dvādaśakalātmane arghapātrāya namaḥ*. Then, having filled the vessel for the *argha* offering together with scents, flowers, and unbroken rice grains...

Oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ maṃ, salutations to the lunar mandala consisting of sixteen digits. Having placed a triangle above that, one should then display the lotus mudrā, the conch mudrā, the cow mudrā, and the mudrās for invocation and so forth. Then...
One should worship with the root mantra seven times, accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains.
Now, for the worship of the mandala: having drawn a triangle, a twelve-petaled lotus, and a square mandala with vermilion (*sindūra*), one should recite within the center of the triangle:
*oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hreṃ hroṃ hraḥ sūryāya sahasrakiraṇāya bodhaśaktisahitāya āgaccha (2) viśa (2) arghopacārāṇi gṛhṇa (2) hūṃ (3) phaṭ (3)*.
Svāhā!
Meditative concentration.
Red in color, with two arms, and seated upon a red lotus;
holding two lotuses and possessing the form of a circle of light, he should be visualized.
Then follows the twelve-petaled worship.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, homage to the Sun (3). Homage to the Lord of Radiance (3). Homage to Bhāskara (3).

Salutation to Dinakara (the Sun). (3) Salutation to Tapana (the Heator). (3) Salutation to Tamovairin (the Enemy of Darkness). (3) Salutation to Caṇḍaraśmi (the One with Fierce Rays). (3) Salutation to Vareṇya (the Most Excellent). (3) Salutation to Bhagavat (the Blessed One). (3) Salutation to Prakāśa (the Illuminator). (3)

Homage to the one with the lotus in hand (3). Thaṃ, homage to Śakra, the wielder of the discus (3). Aṃ, to Aruṇa, whose form is awakening, the teacher of the world: be present in this maṇḍala (2), svāhā! Oṃ (2), to Indra, the thousand-eyed one, who holds the thunderbolt in his hand.
To the one whose vehicle is Airāvata, who is yellow in color, accompanied by Indrāṇī and the Śakti weapon: come!

(2) Accept these offerings of *argha*! (2) Svāhā! Oṃ (2) To Agni, the bearer of oblations, accompanied by the Śakti, the seven-tongued one, red in color. Oṃ (2) To Yama, whose vehicle is the buffalo, who holds the staff of Time (*kāladaṇḍa*) in his hand.

To Dharmarāja, who is accompanied by Ugraśakti and is the ender of life; Oṃ, to Nairṛtya, whose vehicle is a preta, who holds a sword in his hand, the lord of the asuras, accompanied by Kālaśakti; Oṃ, to Varuṇa, the lord of waters, whose vehicle is a makara, who holds a noose in his hand, accompanied by Prāṇaśakti; Oṃ Yāṃ.

In the northwest: to the Lord of Breath, who has a spotted deer as his vehicle, who is green in color, who holds a banner in his hand, and who is accompanied by Caṇḍaśakti. Oṃ Kūṃ! To Kubera, the Lord of the Moon, who has a horse as his vehicle, who holds a jewel in his hand, and who is accompanied by Caṇḍaśakti and Apsarases. Oṃ! To Īśāna, who has a bull as his vehicle.
To the one with a trident in hand, white in color, accompanied by Gaurī; [in the center:
Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, to Brahmā, seated upon the lotus, four-faced, accompanied by the Śakti Gāyatrī, holding a rosary and a book, in the center of this maṇḍala.

Accept the offerings of *argha*, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, who has Garuḍa as his seat, holds the conch and discus in his hands, and is accompanied by Lakṣmī; to Īśvara, who has a corpse as his vehicle, holds the trident and conch in his hands, is accompanied by Lakṣmī, and is joined with Ardhanārī—thus [to him] together with his retinue.
May the Ocean, together with his vehicle and weapons, being worshipped with all ritual offerings, be pleased.
In this maṇḍala, there are the sixteen services (upacāras), consisting of perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.

Having performed one hundred and eight recitations with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should draw a square mandala on the left side of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Having established a triangle in the center, one should offer a flower, saying: "Kṣāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Field (*kṣetrādhipati*). Then, taking the vessel for the offering water (*arghapātra*) and purifying it with incense, [one prepares] the sacrificial oblation (*bali*).

One should offer: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrāṃ vaṃ, may Vaṭuka accept this bali! (2) Svāhā!* (3) *Kṣāṃ, may Kṣetrapāla accept this bali! (2) Svāhā!* (3) *Yāṃ, may the Yoginīs accept this bali! (2) Svāhā!* Thus ends the worship of Sūrya.
Now follows the worship of Heramba.
Whenever one begins the mantra, at that very time one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
The practitioner of mantra should perform the desired rites with the water-pot for the sake of attaining the goal of the mantra.
Oṃ gaḥ astrāya phaṭ. [The seat upon the palms of the hands: Oṃ gūṃ, obeisance to the seat of Heramba. Oṃ gūṃ, obeisance to the form of Heramba. Oṃ, obeisance to Heramba. [With joined palms:
Oṃ gāṃ, obeisance to the heart. Oṃ gīṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ gūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Oṃ gaiṃ...
HŪM for the armor. OṂ GAUṂ VAUṢAṬ for the three eyes. OṂ GAḤ PHAṬ for the weapon. (4) Thus is the ritual placement of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa).
Now, meditation.
The deity seated upon a lion, five-faced and elephant-headed.
He has ten arms and three eyes, and his radiance is equal to that of refined gold.
The giver of grace and fearlessness, holding a vessel filled with sweetmeats.
Having seized the radiant wealth with his hand, he gave it to the Brahmin.
Likewise, he holds a water-pot, a rosary of beads, and a sharp axe.
The auspicious god, holding a noose and a goad, possessing a protruding belly.

Now the mantra: Oṃ hāṃ namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ, O Lord of all obstacles, bestower of all accomplishments, for the pacification of all obstacles! Come, come, O Blessed One, essence of all! Svāhāṃ! Stambha sa-staṃ bhaga hrīṃ hūṃ yāṃ namaḥ svāhā! One should display the mudrās for the invocation and other rites.

Now, the worship of the *argha* vessel: [one should draw] a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square. Then, having established the support (*ādhāra*) in the center of the square, [one recites]: "Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutations to the Support-Energy (*ādhāra-śakti*), to the fire-mandala, whose self consists of the ten digits (*kalā*). Then, having established the vessel [upon it]: (3)

Salutation to the solar disc (*sūrya-maṇḍala*), the vessel consisting of twelve digits (*kalā*). (3) Salutation to the lunar disc (*soma-maṇḍala*), salutation to that which consists of sixteen digits. Then, the cow gesture (*dhenu-mudrā*), the lotus gesture (*padma-mudrā*), and the conch gesture (*śaṅkha-mudrā*).
The invocation mudrā. Then the five jewels. Then one should propitiate [the deity] seven times with the root mantra.
Then follows the Nyāsa of Gaṇeśa: Oṃ hauṃ aṃ, salutation to Vighneśa. (2) Āṃ, salutation to Vighnarāja.

(2) Iṃ, salutation to Vināyaka. (2) Īṃ, salutation to Śivātman. (2) Uṃ, salutation to Vighnakartṛ. (2) Ūṃ, salutation to Vighnahartṛ. (2) Ṛṃ, salutation to Gaṇanāyaka. (2) Ṝṃ, salutation to Ekadanta. (2) Ḷṃ...

Salutation to Vidantāya. (2) Ḷi, salutation to Gajavaktrāya. (2) Eṃ, salutation to Nirañjanāya. (2) Aiṃ, salutation to Kapardine. (2) Oṃ, salutation to Dīrghajihvāya. (2) Auṃ, salutation to Śaṅkhakaṇṭhāya. (2) Aṃ, salutation to Vṛṣadhvajāya. (2) Aḥ, salutation to Gaṇanāthāya. (2) Kaṃ, salutation to Gajendrāya. (2)
Khaṃ, salutation to Śūrpakarṇa. (2) Gaṃ, salutation to Trilocana. (2) Ghaṃ, salutation to Lambodara.
(2) Ṅaṃ, salutation to Mahānanda. (2) Caṃ, salutation to Caturmukha. (2) Chaṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva. (2) Jaṃ, salutation to Āmoda. (2) Jhaṃ, salutation to Durmukha. (2) Ñaṃ, salutation to Sumukha.

Namaḥ. Ṭaṃ, obeisance to Pramoda. (2) Ṭhaṃ, obeisance to Ekapāda. (2) Ḍaṃ, obeisance to Vijihva. (2) Ḍhaṃ, obeisance to Śūra. (2) Ṇaṃ, obeisance to Vīra. (2) Taṃ, obeisance to Ṣaṇmukha. (2) Thaṃ, obeisance to Varada. (2) Daṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva. (2)

Dhaṃ, homage to Vakratuṇḍa. (2) Naṃ, homage to Dviraṇḍa. (2) Paṃ, homage to Senānī. (2) Phaṃ, homage to Grāmiṇī. Vaṃ, homage to Mantra. (2) Bhaṃ, homage to Vimantra. Maṃ, homage to Mahāvāha. (2) Yaṃ, homage to Jaṭila. (2) Raṃ, homage to Muṇḍin. (2) Laṃ, homage to Khaṇḍin.

Namaḥ. (2) Vaṃ, salutation to the one worthy of choice; (2) Śaṃ, salutation to the one whose banner is the bull; Ṣaṃ, salutation to the beloved of Bhava; (2) Saṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśa; (2) Haṃ, salutation to the one who sounds like a ram; (2) Laṃ, salutation to the all-pervading one; (2) Kṣaṃ, salutation to the Lord of the Gaṇas. Thus one should perform the placement [of these syllables] in the locations of the Mātṛkās.
Resembling the young morning sun, with the face of an elephant and three eyes.
Holding a noose, a goad, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands, and joined with Śakti.
Thus, one should worship the deities of the placement (nyāsa) within forty-nine squares; [the central deity] is in the center.
One should worship Heraṃba with the root mantra. Then [offer] the bali with the root mantra of Heraṃba.
Then one should recite the King of Hymns (Stavarāja).
Now follows the worship of Śiva.
Now, the root mantra: Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hskhphreṃ hsraiṃ aghore hrāṃ ghore hrīṃ ghoraghoratare hrūṃ hraiṃ sarvataḥ sarvasarve hrauṃ namaste rudrarūpe hraḥ. (5)

Hskṣmlvryūṃ Śkṣmlvryūṃ. I worship the venerable sandals of Svacchandabhairava together with Bhairavī, in the center of the pericarp. Then follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): Aghore Hrāṃ, salutation to the heart. Thaghore Hrīṃ, svāhā to the head. Ghoraghoratare Hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Sarvata... [etc.]
Savasarve hraiṃ, for the armor, hūṃ. Homage to you in the form of Rudra, hrauṃ, for the three eyes, vauṣaṭ.
hsrauṁ hskhphreṁ śrīṁ hrīṁ aiṁ hraḥ astāya phaṭ || (4) ||
Now, meditation.
Dark blue like the petal of a blue lotus, with five faces, he stands upon a corpse.
Clad in a tiger skin, with earrings upon his ears.
He is beautiful, wearing a necklace of serpents, and resplendent with the Kaula power.
He had ten arms, great splendor, and three eyes in each face.
Abounding with an elephant hide as a sacred thread, and adorned with ornaments of serpents.
The god who wears a garland of severed heads and is adorned with serpent ornaments.
White, yellow, red, dark-blue, and tawny—these are the five [colors].
In this way, O Great Goddess, one should meditate upon the God, the Lord who is the crest-jewel of the gods.
In the left [hands], there is a bell, a mirror, a trident, a sword, and a hand-drum (ḍamaru).
And the nāga king Māla, holding a spear, a javelin, and a club.
Licking everything, it is saluted by all the gods.
In this manner, one should cause [the breath] to flow equally; this is according to another tradition.
In some places it was red, likewise blue, and in some places resembling cow's milk.
In some instances, one should contemplate the great god Aghora as yellow.

Having thus invoked [the deity] into that maṇḍala, and having performed the rites of stabilization (saṃsthāpana) and so forth while displaying the mudrās, one should then begin the worship of the cakra. It consists of a triangle, a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, a square with four doors, and then four corners.
For the worship of the four corners: Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. [In the] northwest.

(3) *Kṣīṃ*, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla; in the southeast. (3) Obeisance to Draṣṭeśvara; in the southwest. (3) Obeisance to Caṇḍeśvara; in the northeast. (3) Obeisance to Nandin; at the northern gate. (3) Obeisance to Mahākāla; at the southern gate. (3) Obeisance to Bhṛṅgin; at the western gate. (3) Obeisance to Kuṣmāṇḍa.
Homage! At the eastern gate: thus [they bear] their respective colors and their respective weapons. Then follows the worship of the eight petals.
I worship the sandals of the goddess Brahmāṇī. (5) Māheśvarī. (5) Kaumārī. (5) Vaiṣṇavī. (5) Vārāhī. (5) Indrāṇī. (5) Cāmuṇḍā. (5) Mahālakṣmī.

[They bear] their respective colors and their respective weapons. Then follows the worship of the hexagon: (5) I worship the sandals of the goddess Rati; (5) the goddess Prīti; (5) the goddess Manobhavā; (5) the goddess Subhagā; (5) the goddess Manoramā; (5) the goddess Ānandanī. [All are] entirely red in color and four-armed.
One should meditate on her as holding a skull, a trident, and displaying the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons. This is the worship of the triangle: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
In the center of the triangle, worship is performed with the previously mentioned mantra. The meditation on the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is as previously described.
Now follows the meditation on the Supreme Goddess (Parameśvarī).
Then Kāla, dark as a great cloud, with six faces, eighteen eyes, and twelve broad, vine-like arms, [seized] the Pārijāta tree, which was reddened by the sap of glowing resin and made of gold.

With the tips of his six hands, he holds the noose, the gestures of fearlessness and boon, the rosary, the skull-cup, the uplifted conch, the mirror of pure luster like a stainless petal, and the garland of severed heads. (1)
Seated upon a lion-throne, her lotus-feet delighting with anklets, with Karkoṭaka bound as her girdle, and Takṣaka’s necklace adorning her upper body, she is most beautiful.

The moonstones are like earrings fastened to their ears, the luster of conchs is their earrings, the ruby-streaks are upon their brow-crests, and the great serpents with rubies on their heads are upon their faces.
With his topknot and earrings, with bracelets formed by black serpents, with armlets upon his fingers,
and with necklaces consisting of rows of serpent-jewels, his ornaments take on a dancing form.

O Kubjikā, who wears a garland of fire-flames, whose hair is like the peacock feathers of a blazing crest, who is adorned with a necklace of severed heads, who bestows fearlessness and removes all misfortune—salutations to you! (1)
Thus one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess in the center of the triangle. (5)
[Thus ends the ritual manual for the worship of Lalitasvacchanda.]
[Now, the worship of the guru-maṇḍala.]
Then follows the worship of the ten directions beginning with Indra.

(5) To the great sacred field of Prayāga, to Aṁ Aśitāṅgabhairava, accompanied by Āṁ Brahmāṇī, I worship the venerable sandals. (5) To the great sacred field of Vārāṇasī, to Īṁ Rurubhairava, accompanied by Īṁ...

To Maheśvarī together with [her consort], (5) to the great sacred field of Kolāpura, uṃ to Caṇḍabhairava together with Kaumārī, (5) to the great sacred field of Aṭṭahāsa, ṛṃ to Krodhabhairava together with Vaiṣṇavī.

(5) To Jayantī, the Great Field, ḶṂ; to Unmattabhairava, accompanied by Vārāhī, ḸṂ. (5) To Caritra, the Great Field, EṂ; to Kapālabhairava, accompanied by Indrāṇī, AIṂ. (5) To Ekāmra, the Great Field, OṂ; to Bhīṣaṇabhairava, accompanied by Cāmuṇḍā, AUṂ.
To the one accompanied by [his consort] || (5) To the goddess Koṭa Mahākṣetra, to Aṃ Saṃhārabhairava, to Aḥ Mahālakṣmī, and to the one accompanied by her, obeisance! Meditation on Bhairava.

Bhairava should be meditated upon as having four arms, being black in color, possessing three eyes, and having disheveled hair standing erect; he is embraced by his consort Sarvadevī at the breasts, and holds a trident, a banner, a skull, and a chopper in his hands, with his hand resting on her chin.
One should worship within the petals of the eight-petaled lotus, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.

This manuscript was transcribed in the year 1979 from an ancient palm-leaf manuscript by Śrī Mad Rājaguru Hemarāja Paṇḍita through Śāradāvilāsa Śarmā.
